hero.name: Siddharth
hero.who: a production manager at a Tiruppur garment factory, busy all day but achieving little

story.b: Siddharth is the production manager at a garment export unit in Tiruppur that makes T-shirts for foreign brands. His phone rings from seven in the morning. A machine is down on line four. A supplier is late with dye. The cutting master wants leave. A buyer wants a video call. Siddharth runs between floors, signs papers, settles fights and answers sixty WhatsApp messages before lunch. He goes home at nine, too tired to talk to his wife Kavya or their son. On Friday the owner, Mr Sundaram, asks a simple question: what improved on the floor this month? Siddharth opens his mouth and finds nothing to say. A big shipment is still running late, and he has been busy every minute.

ask.q: Siddharth is busy every minute but cannot name one real improvement. What is the most useful shift for him?
o: Work even longer hours so more things get done
Focus on getting the right things done, not just many things
Wait for a less hectic season before changing anything
ask.why: Longer hours add more busyness, not more results, and calm seasons rarely arrive in a factory. Effectiveness means choosing and finishing the work that actually changes outcomes. That shift turns his effort into something he can point to.

chapters.take: Being busy is not the same as being effective.

story.b: That weekend, Siddharth thinks about his old manager in Chennai, who always seemed calm and on top of things. Siddharth had always assumed some people were simply born like that. Now he wonders. Maybe calm and effective is a set of habits, not a personality. On Monday he tries one simple thing. Instead of listing his daily tasks, he writes down the main result he is actually responsible for: shipments leaving on time, with no quality rejections. He tapes it above his desk. He also notices that Murugan, the supervisor on line four, makes dozens of decisions daily that affect that same result. Murugan is not a manager, but in a real sense he runs a small part of the factory.

ask.q: Murugan says planning habits are only for big bosses, not line supervisors like him. What should Siddharth tell him?
o: He is right, supervisors should only follow orders
Only very talented people can become effective anyway
Anyone whose decisions affect results can learn these habits, including him
ask.why: Effectiveness is a set of habits, not a gift reserved for top bosses or naturally brilliant people. Murugan's daily choices shape quality and deadlines. Seeing himself as responsible for results, and practising the habits, can make him far more useful.

chapters.take: Effectiveness is a habit anyone can learn, not a talent some are born with.

story.b: Siddharth buys a small pocket diary from the stationery shop near the bus stand. For one week, every hour, he writes down what he actually did. On Saturday he reads it over a filter coffee and is shocked. He spent almost two hours a day in meetings where he only listened. Another hour went to signing small purchase slips that his assistant could sign. The rest was cut into tiny pieces by phone calls, so he never had more than fifteen minutes to think. He makes three changes. He drops two meetings. He lets his assistant approve slips below five thousand rupees. And he blocks two to four every afternoon, phone on silent, to plan the next week's production.

ask.q: Kavya, a school vice principal, says she never has time for the new timetable. What should she try first?
o: Record how she actually spends each hour for a week, then cut the waste
Wake up an hour earlier and squeeze it in
Trust her memory of where her day goes and just try harder
ask.why: Memory is a poor guide to where time goes, so trying harder or squeezing in extra hours misses the leaks. A simple record shows the waste clearly, and gathering the freed time into one long block gives real thinking work the stretch it needs.

chapters.take: Track where your time really goes. Memory lies, a diary does not.

story.b: In his first quiet afternoon block, Siddharth asks himself a new question. Not how hard he is working, but what he could contribute that would really change results for the factory. He goes back through the last ten late shipments. He expected to find slow machines. Instead, seven were late because samples went back and forth with buyers three or four times. The measurement sheets were confusing, and nobody owned the process. He spends two weeks designing a clear one-page specification sheet and makes one person responsible for tracking each sample. He also asks Mr Sundaram which result matters most to him. The answer surprises him: fewer rejections, even more than faster lines. Siddharth changes his priorities to match.

ask.q: Priya, a junior in the merchandising team, works hard but feels invisible. What question would help her most?
o: How can I look busier when the owner walks past?
How can I get a bigger title before anything else?
What contribution from me would actually change results for the team?
ask.why: Looking busy and chasing a title both focus on her image, not on outcomes. Asking what she could contribute turns her attention outward, to the results that matter, which makes her work more meaningful and far more visible.

chapters.take: Ask what you can contribute to results, not how busy you look.

story.b: The factory needs a new quality head. The obvious choice is Anand, who is neat, punctual and great with reports, but rarely spots a defect. Then there is Selvi, a checker on line two who can find a crooked seam from three metres away, but whose paperwork is a mess. The old Siddharth would have picked the safe all-rounder. Now he asks what each person does really well. He makes Selvi quality head and moves Anand beside her to handle reports and records. Within a month, rejections drop and the reports are tidy. He looks at himself the same way. He is good at fixing problems on the floor, not at polished buyer presentations, so he hands those to the merchandising lead, who loves them.

ask.q: Siddharth's young engineer is brilliant at fixing machines but hopeless at planning schedules. What is the best way to use him?
o: Send him on planning courses until he stops being weak there
Let him focus on machines and pair him with a good planner
Move him to planning so he becomes more well-rounded
ask.why: Spending years fixing weaknesses usually produces someone average, and moving him to planning wastes a clear strength. Giving him work that uses his gift, and pairing him with someone strong where he is weak, gets the best results for everyone.

chapters.take: Build on what people do well, and cover their weak spots with a partner.

story.h: Five projects, one at a time
story.b: By now Siddharth has started five improvement projects at once: new software, the sample system, a canteen upgrade, a training plan and a monthly report for the owner. Each moves a few inches a week. He decides to finish the sample system first and pause the rest. He also stops the monthly report after learning nobody has read it in a year. Then a big decision arrives. Mr Sundaram wants to buy an expensive new cutting machine. Before giving his view, Siddharth calls Selvi, Murugan and the cutting master and asks them to argue against it. They raise a problem he had missed: the machine would block the loading bay. Together they find a better spot before anything is ordered.

ask.q: Siddharth has five half-finished projects and a big decision coming. What is the most effective approach?
o: Finish the most important project first, drop what no longer helps, and invite disagreement before deciding
Push all five projects equally so none is neglected
Decide the big question quickly himself so the team is not distracted
ask.why: Pushing everything at once keeps every project half-done, and deciding alone misses problems others can see. Concentrating on one priority, stopping work that adds nothing and hearing real disagreement first lead to fewer, better decisions.

chapters.take: Do the most important thing first, one at a time, and stop what no longer helps.

story.b: Six months later, the Tiruppur unit ships on time for the first time in two years. Rejections are down, two nearby factories have copied the sample sheets, and Selvi has trained three new checkers. Siddharth's phone still rings, but less, because Murugan and his assistant now settle most small things themselves. His afternoon block is guarded like a buyer meeting. Most evenings he is home by seven, playing carrom with his son before dinner. One Friday, Mr Sundaram asks the same question as before: what improved this month? This time Siddharth hands him a single page with three lines on it. Mr Sundaram reads it twice and asks him to teach the other managers how he did it.

chapters.take: Fewer chosen tasks, done well, achieved more than endless busyness ever did.
